rationale: The item asks whether dental fear led the respondent to put off making an appointment, which is a delay in scheduling that happens before a dental visit.
The item asks whether dental fear has led to canceling or failing to appear for a dental appointment, which matches the cancellation/no-show avoidance class.
Muscle tension is a bodily change in response to a stimulus, so the item fits the physiological arousal question class; the embarrassment subclass does not apply.
An increase in breathing rate is a bodily change in response to a stimulus, so the item is a physiological arousal question; no more specific child class fits.
Perspiring is a bodily change in response to a stimulus, so it falls under physiological arousal; no more specific class such as embarrassment applies.
Nausea and an upset stomach are bodily changes in response to a stimulus, so the item fits physiological arousal; no more specific child class covers it.
A faster heartbeat is a change in bodily state in response to a stimulus, which is physiological arousal; no more specific child class fits.
The item asks about fear when making a dental appointment, which is anticipatory fear about something that happens before a dental visit.
The item asks about fear of approaching the dentist's office, which happens before the dental visit and is one of the specific dental-situation stimuli rated in dental fear surveys.
The item asks directly about a patient sitting in a waiting room, which matches this class exactly.
Being seated in the dental chair happens during the dental visit and is a specific dental stimulus, though not a procedure.
The item asks about fear of a specific sensory stimulus, the smell of the dental office, which the patient encounters during a dental visit.
Seeing the dentist walk in is a specific dental stimulus that elicits fear, and it occurs during the dental visit.
Seeing the anesthetic needle is fear of a specific dental stimulus that occurs during a dental visit.
The item asks about fear of a specific dental stimulus, the anesthetic needle injection, which occurs during a dental procedure.
Seeing the drill is a fear-provoking dental stimulus tied to the tooth drilling procedure.
The item is about fear of a specific dental stimulus, the sound of the drill, which is tied to the tooth drilling procedure.
The item asks about a specific dental stimulus, the drill's vibrations, experienced during a tooth drilling procedure.
The item refers directly to a tooth cleaning procedure performed during a dental visit, so the tooth cleaning procedure question class is the most specific match.
The item asks about overall fear of undergoing dental work, which is a fear of a medical procedure and specifically concerns dental procedures.
The item asks about anticipatory anxiety felt in the time just before a dental visit.
The item is about generally avoiding dental visits, not specifically about canceling, missing, or delaying appointments, so the dental visit avoidance class is the most specific fit.
The item asks about nervousness in anticipation of upcoming dental visits, so it is both an anticipatory fear question and a question about the time before a dental visit.
The item asks about fear that something bad would happen if one visited a dentist, which is anticipatory fear; no more specific class covers this catastrophic expectation.

The item asks about general fear felt while visiting the dentist, which fits the class for questions about what happens during a dental visit, since it names no specific stimulus, procedure, pain, or avoidance.

A faster heartbeat when going to the dentist is a bodily change in response to a stimulus, which is physiological arousal; the timing (on the way or during the visit) is too unclear to also add a during-visit or prior-to-visit class.
The item asks about delaying the scheduling of dental appointments, which matches the class for questions about delay in scheduling a dental appointment.
The item describes anticipatory worry about what might go wrong before a dental visit, so it fits both the pre-visit class and the anticipatory fear class, which has no more specific matching child.
The item asks whether dental visits are actively avoided (dental visit avoidance) or endured with intense fear while the visit takes place (during dental visit).
The item asks how long the respondent has feared going to the dentist, which is anticipatory fear of a dental visit; no more specific class covers fear duration.
The item asks how avoidance of dental visits affects the respondent's life, and it explicitly names embarrassment about the appearance of the teeth or mouth as one consequence.
The item describes anticipatory fear of going to the dentist, driven by worry about a panic attack whose physical symptoms (sweating, pounding heart, chest pain) are physiological arousal.
The item is about fear of going to the dentist (anticipatory fear) caused by social self-consciousness and fear of being judged, which is closest to embarrassment.

The item asks about anxiety over painful or uncomfortable procedures, which fits fear of pain (no severity specified) and fear of undergoing a procedure; OHD_0008044 (dental procedure question) is a reasonable alternative if the dental-visit setting should be captured.
The item asks about anxiety over feeling embarrassed or ashamed when visiting the dentist, which fits the embarrassment class and the during-dental-visit context.
The item asks about anxiety over losing control of what happens while at the dentist, which is about the dental visit itself, and no more specific class covers loss of control.
The item asks about anxiety over feeling sick, queasy or disgusted, a change in bodily state, experienced while at the dentist.
The item asks about anxiety over a specific dental stimulus, the numbness from local anesthetic, which is experienced during the dental visit.

The item asks about anxiety during the dental visit over not knowing what the dentist will do, which is anticipatory fear of an undergone procedure; the more specific dental procedure class (OHD_0008044) is a plausible alternative, but no particular procedure is named.
No class covers cost, so this best fits as anticipatory anxiety about the expense of treatment, felt in the context of going to the dentist.
The item asks about anxiety toward needles or injections, a specific dental stimulus that is also part of a dental procedure during the visit.
The item asks about fear of a specific dental-related stimulus, gagging or choking, which happens during a dental visit.
The item asks about anxiety toward a specific dental stimulus, an unsympathetic or unkind dentist, which is encountered during a dental visit.
The item asks how the respondent would feel the day before a dental treatment visit, which is anticipatory fear about something that happens before the visit.
The item asks about feelings while sitting in the waiting room before treatment, which is the waiting-room situation plus fear in anticipation of treatment.
The item asks about anticipatory feelings toward having a tooth drilled, which is both a tooth drilling procedure and a specific feared dental stimulus.
The item asks how the respondent would feel about to undergo scaling and polishing, which is a tooth cleaning procedure.
The item asks about anticipatory feelings toward a local anaesthetic injection, which is both a specific dental procedure and a specific feared dental stimulus.
